notes:
Summary: ByteFlux builds a multi-language IDE copilot plugin used by product teams and enterprise customers. Primary requirement is keystroke-level streaming with predictable Time-To-First-Token (TTFT) for single-line completions and low jitter for interactive typing. They also need model/version pinning so in-product beta users see deterministic behavior.

Key technical targets (customer):
- TTFT target: 30-80ms median for inline single-token streaming; 95th percentile <150-200ms for short completions (<=32 tokens).
- Jitter goal: <20ms median inter-token variance during steady typing; spikes tolerated up to 200ms only for cold starts.
- Backpressure: client must apply soft backpressure when server queueing seen; prefer low-latency fallbacks (distilled model) instead of big tail latencies.
- Token budgets: default inline suggestion cap 16 tokens, multi-line snippet up to 64 tokens; want ability to tune per-route by file type and user tier.
- Model strategy: pin lightweight distilled model for most completions; route to larger models for complex refactors or long-form generation. Automated fallback routing required when Dedicated capacity saturated.
- Observability: per-keystroke latency histogram, token emission rate, batch sizes, KV cache hit rates.

POC specifics:
- Running Redwood hosted API with a simulated Dedicated pool (burst config) to reproduce contention scenarios.
- Tests done with our IDE harness (internal) measuring keystroke intervals, emulated multi-user sessions (50-200 concurrent).
- Initial metrics: median TTFT ~55ms OK, but 95p latency at ~220ms; jitter spikes during short bursts when batching thresholds kick in. Primary hypothesis: suboptimal batching thresholds + lack of token budget enforcement at gateway.

Engineering asks from Redwood:
- Guidance on continuous batching thresholds for keystroke workloads (suggested: aggressive 0-3ms hold + async flush on user pause).
- Mechanisms to enforce per-request token budgets and early stop signals for streaming responses to prevent client-side backpressure cascades.
- Example routing policy for model pinning + fallback (distilled -> base -> large) with SLA-based preemption.
- Instrumentation hooks: streaming trace ids per completion, inter-token timing logs, per-user backlog size.

Commercial/Procurement notes:
- Cost sensitivity: careful about per-token costs for high-DAU IDEs; they expect optimize recommendations (quantization, batching) to shave ~30-50% token cost.
- Security: must pass KMS integration and SSO (SAML) before production access. Data residency: EU customers require routing to eu region for workspace-specific data.

Quotes & snippets from calls:
- "If users feel the assistant lag, retention drops — we need keystroke-level responsiveness." — Head of Product
- "Prefer deterministic pinning for our beta cohort, but want automatic fallback when capacity hits thresholds." — Lead SW Eng

Next steps (short):
- Agree on POC success metrics (median TTFT, 95p, jitter percentiles) and thresholds by 2026-03-05 (ACTION: Maya + Ravi + ByteFlux eng).
- SE to deliver tuning guide with batching/backpressure recommendations and a proxy config sample by 2026-03-12.
- Security team to review KMS integration checklist; Redwood to provide template IAM roles and HSM options.

Open blockers: security checklist items, cost model for high-DAU token budgets, final SLA for Dedicated bursts.
